1:
How long the ark had lain neglected frames the chapter. Henry observes that nothing has been heard of it since Kirjath-jearim but the once when Saul called for it, so what had made so great a figure was thrown aside as a neglected thing; he draws the lesson that perpetual visibility is no mark of the true church, God being present with his people even when they want the outward tokens. Delitzsch puts a figure on it, about seventy years in Abinadab's house, and uses the span to explain how Uzzah and Ahio can still be called his sons; Ellicott says more loosely, more than two generations. On the muster Gill notes that the Greek gives seventy thousand where the Targum and Syriac keep the Hebrew's thirty.

Two textual knots come early. Delitzsch defends Baale-Jehudah as a place name against the ancient versions and Luther, who took it appellatively as the rulers or citizens of Judah, since the following word thence is unintelligible otherwise. Clarke and Ellicott identify it with Kirjath-jearim, Ellicott adding that either from should be read to or the historian has passed over the outward journey, and canvassing two sites, each three or four hours' march from the capital. On the clause about the name Clarke suspects a scribal doubling, the second occurrence probably to be read there, so the sense is that there the name of the Lord of hosts was invoked; Ellicott keeps both and translates, which is called by the name, the name of Jehovah of hosts.

The cart is where they differ most, though all grant it broke the law that the ark be borne on Levites' shoulders. Clarke allows the new cart was used through respect but says flatly that neglect of the proper carriage caused Uzzah's death. Ellicott is gentlest: the new cart was doubtless meant as a mark of respect, and it is not necessary to suppose David intended any violation, since the ark having lain neglected so long the exact requirements may easily have passed out of mind. Gill and Wesley blame the Philistine precedent and refuse it as an excuse, Gill finding it strange that so many priests and Levites, and David so versed in the law, did not consult it, Wesley putting the principle exactly: God might wink at the Philistines because they were ignorant of his laws, yet be angry with Israel for the same act, because they knew or might have known. Henry's version is the memorable one, that Philistines may cart the ark with impunity but Israelites do so at their peril, and old or new the cart was not what God appointed; he wonders how so wise and good a man came to be guilty of such an oversight, and charitably hopes it was because he was so intent upon the substance of the service that he forgot the circumstance. Wesley adds that their joy made them inconsiderate.

Delitzsch finds a third knot in the music. The Hebrew says all manner of woods of cypress, which can only mean instruments of cypress wood, and even then the expression would be very strange; Chronicles reads with all their might and with songs, which he takes for the correct reading from which our text has sprung, noting that the Greek combines the two. Henry takes the rejoicing for his subject: it might well put them into a transport to see the ark rise out of obscurity towards a public station, and as secret worship is better the more secret it is, so public worship is better the more public; but public joy must always be as before the Lord, and not degenerate into what is carnal. He passes on the suggestion that David wrote the sixty-eighth psalm for the occasion, since it opens with Moses' prayer at the removing of the ark and notices the singers and the princes of the tribes.
6:
What the oxen did is not agreed. Delitzsch says they slipped; Henry reports the critics divided, the margin having them stumble, some that they kicked against the goad, some that they stuck in the mire; Ellicott offers a suggestion nobody else makes, that they turned aside to snatch the scattered grain of the floor. The floor's name divides them the same way. Gill takes Nachon and the Chidon of the parallel for two names of one man or place. Delitzsch and Ellicott both doubt it is a personal name: Delitzsch renders it the threshingfloor of the stroke and supposes the name came from the incident rather than an owner, while Ellicott says the place is entirely unknown.

Why the penalty was so heavy is the chapter's question. Henry gives several reasons: the touching was forbidden on pain of death, so God would show how he might have dealt with our first parents; he saw the presumption of Uzzah's heart, familiarity even with what is most awful being apt to breed contempt;he saw too that a good intention will not justify a bad action, since it will not suffice to say of what is ill done that it was well meant. Ellicott agrees that what seems an exceedingly severe penalty for a well-meaning though unlawful act was on reflection a necessary manifestation of displeasure, involving not only a breach of the letter, of which David was equally guilty, but a disposition to profane familiarity with sacred things. Wesley argues from the general good: men are improper judges of God's actions, and it is reasonable he should make examples against sins seemingly small, so there is more of mercy than of justice in such acts, the justice confined to one person while the benefit is common to mankind in all future ages.

On Uzzah's own case the two who raise it differ in nerve. Ellicott stops carefully short: judgments of this kind were temporal and give no indication in themselves of the offender's treatment beyond the grave. Clarke goes the whole way: Uzzah sinned through ignorance and precipitancy, having no time to reflect when the oxen stumbled, and no man can doubt of his eternal safety, since he committed a sin unto death but the mercy of God was doubtless extended to his soul. David's displeasure divides them again. Henry is severe: it is not said David was angry because Uzzah had affronted God but because God had made a breach upon Uzzah, the very word used of God's own anger; David did not then act like a man after God's own heart, and when we lie under God's anger we must keep under our own. Ellicott defends him: the cause was the judgment, but it does not follow he was angry with God, being simply disturbed at so untoward an interruption of his plans. Wesley makes it grief, for the sin and for the heavy stroke by which their hopes were dashed.

The fear that followed is read as excess or as the point of the whole. Henry thinks David should rather have said, let the ark come to me and I will take warning, though he allows the fear may be a good use of the judgment. Ellicott takes it as the intended effect, producing the awe in which they had been deficient, and adds that if at first excessive it was soon moderated. On Obed-edom they agree. Ellicott establishes that he was a Levite, called the Gittite from a Levitical city. Wesley makes the contrast: he knew what slaughter the ark had made among the Philistines and at Bethshemesh, had seen Uzzah struck dead, and yet opened his doors without fear, knowing it a savour of death only to those who treated it ill. Clarke draws the rule, that whoever entertains God's messengers or consecrates his house to his service will infallibly be blessed.
12:
The carriage is put right first: Gill notes that David had seen the mistake and ordered the Levites to bear the ark on their shoulders with the staves, Ellicott that he no longer presumed to violate the law. On the sacrifices Ellicott corrects a common notion: it is unnecessary to suppose offerings were made at every six steps, for although possible it is not recorded; David sacrificed when the removal had been successfully begun and again when the journey was done, so the work was begun and ended with solemn sacrifice, offered through the priests.

The dancing is where they separate. Gill reports that the Targum renders it praised before the Lord with all his might, that the Greek and Syriac agree, and that Castel approved this since it nowhere appears to have been a custom to dance before the ark; he grants that a later writer shows dancing the proper sense, and himself takes it of leaping and skipping as a lamb. Delitzsch and Ellicott both notice who usually danced: it was an expression of holy enthusiasm from time immemorial, from the song at the Red Sea onwards, but in every such celebration none but women are described as taking part, so the king by joining them marked his sense of the occasion and his readiness to do his utmost for God's honour. Wesley normalises it as thankfulness expressed by outward carriage, after the manner of those times. Clarke will not have it: dancing is a religious ceremony among the Hindoos, who consider it an act of devotion to their idols, and it is evident to him that David considered it so; what connection dancing can have with devotion he cannot tell, though he allows that unpremeditated and involuntary skipping may be the effect of sudden mental elation.

The linen ephod divides them on a point of law. Delitzsch calls it strictly a priestly costume, not prescribed in the law for official duties but as denoting the priestly character of the wearer, and has David wear it as head of the priestly nation. Ellicott disputes the assumption. It is usually spoken of as if David were arrayed in a distinctively priestly dress, but the ephod was not prescribed as part of that dress at all, the high priest's being quite a different thing; it was worn by others, as by Samuel, is elsewhere connected with idolatrous worship, and the high priest's was of one material where the garments of ordinary priests and the ephods of Samuel and David were of another. His explanation is that it was simply a garment worn by anyone engaged in religious service, used of the priests because such service was their ordinary life, and so not a peculiarly priestly dress. Wesley keeps the priestly sense but turns it to David's humility, that he laid by his royal robes and put this on to declare that though king he willingly owned himself the Lord's minister and servant.

On Michal two of them notice the same small thing in the text. Delitzsch observes that she is called the daughter of Saul here and not the wife of David, because on this occasion she showed her father's disposition rather than her husband's, and recalls that in Saul's time nobody troubled about the ark. Ellicott draws the same contrast between the spirit of Saul's house in which she was brought up and David's, adding that she had loved him as a brave hero and could not understand the enthusiasm which led him to rank himself among the common people before the Lord. Wesley makes her charge specific, that she despised him as of a base and mean spirit, who knew not how to carry himself with the majesty that became his place; and Clarke notes what she did not do, making no outward reproach but thinking he had disgraced himself and keeping her mind to herself.
20:
The blessing of the household is read practically. Ellicott explains whom it was for, those of the house whom eastern custom barred from the ceremonies, and notes that the scene following is omitted from Chronicles. Henry turns it into a rule for ministers, that public performances do not excuse a man from family worship, and observes that David, though he had prophets and priests for chaplains, did not devolve the work on them but blessed his household himself, since it is angels' work to worship God and can be no disparagement to the greatest of men. He adds the unwelcome corollary, that even the palaces of princes are not exempt from domestic troubles.

What Michal really objected to is Henry's question, and his answer is careful. It was not her covetousness but her pride that made her fret; she pretended to dislike the dancing as a reproach to David's virtue when what displeased her was the diminution of his honour, and so represented his conduct as lewd and immodest. Henry then refuses the charge on the facts: we have no reason to think it true, David no doubt observed decorum and governed his zeal with discretion, and it is common for those who reproach religion to put false colours upon it. He observes too that the contempt began in the heart and only afterwards reached the tongue, and that the exercises of religion appear very mean to those who have little religion themselves. Ellicott calls her speech cutting irony; Wesley has her despise him as of a base and mean spirit, who knew not how to carry himself with the majesty that became his place.

David's reply turns on a tense. The received version has him promise to play before the Lord in future, and Gill, Henry and Wesley take it so, Henry drawing from it that the more we are vilified for well-doing the more resolute we should be, and Wesley repeating almost the same words. Ellicott and Delitzsch read a past instead: rather, have I danced, or, before Jehovah have I played, the verb meaning to joke or give utterance to joy. On the next clause they agree again. Ellicott notes that the Greek, not understanding it, altered base in mine own sight to in thine eyes, and explains that where Michal charged him with making himself base before the maidservants, who were no fit judges, David was ready to abase himself in his own eyes for God's honour; Delitzsch renders it the same way and observes that the reminder of God's choosing him before her father humbles the pride of the king's daughter.

Why Michal had no child is answered three ways. Wesley and Delitzsch make it punishment, Wesley that God justly punished her proud and petulant carriage, Delitzsch that she was humbled by God for her pride. Clarke and Ellicott make it David's doing, Clarke that probably David never more took her to his bed, though allowing that God might have subjected her to a barrenness counted in that country both a misfortune and a reproach, and Ellicott supposing that the long separation during David's outlawry, when she was married to a man deeply attached to her, had estranged them, so that when their different spirit came out David determined on no further intercourse. Gill offers a third reason, from Abarbinel, that it was so ordered in providence that the seed of David and of Saul might not be mixed, and disposes of the children she is elsewhere said to have brought up as adopted or another woman's. Clarke draws the lesson: Michal formed her judgment without reason and meddled with what she did not understand, and we should be careful how we attribute actions whose reasons we cannot comprehend to motives that seem unjustifiable, since rash judgments are doubly pernicious, hurting those who form them and those of whom they are formed.
